Generate The Clinical P-BEST 2024 Pooling Matrix

Source: R/additional_designs.R
pbest_clinical_matrix.Rd

Construct the pseudo-random balanced \(J \times N\) pooling matrix used for the 384-to-94 clinical P-BEST design reported by Zismanov et al. (2024).

Usage

pbest_clinical_matrix(N = 384L, J = 94L, seed = 42L)

Arguments

N

Integer scalar giving the total number of individuals. The default is 384L. In the returned design this is the column dimension \(N\) of \(\mathbf{M}\).

J

Integer scalar giving the total number of pools. The default is 94L. In the returned design this is the row dimension \(J\) of \(\mathbf{M}\).

seed

Integer scalar used to initialize the pseudo-random tie-breaking step. The default is 42L. Different seeds generate different balanced realizations of the same construction heuristic.

Value

A sparse binary matrix of class dgCMatrix with dimensions \(J \times N\). Under the default \((N,J) = (384,94)\) setting, each column sum is seven and each row sum lies in \(\{28,29\}\). The attached design attribute is a named list with fields type, N, J, seed, pools_per_sample, and pool_size_range.

Details

This function targets the clinical design with $$N = 384, \qquad J = 94.$$ The implementation fixes the number of pools per individual at $$w_i = |\mathcal{J}_i| = r = 7$$ and therefore creates $$T = Nr$$ total incidences. For the default parameter values, $$T = 384 \times 7 = 2688.$$ Distributing these incidences over \(J=94\) pools implies an average pool size of \(T/J \approx 28.6\). The construction therefore aims for a nearly balanced row-load profile with $$56 \text{ pools of size } 29 \quad \text{and} \quad 38 \text{ pools of size } 28.$$ The algorithm processes the individuals sequentially and assigns each individual to the currently least-loaded pools, using pseudo-random jitter to break ties. The output is thus a balanced heuristic realization rather than a closed-form algebraic design. It is documented as a package-specific heuristic constructor motivated by the reported clinical matrix dimensions, not as a claim that the exact clinical deployment matrix has been recovered.

References

Zismanov, S., Yelin, I., Klochendler, A., et al. (2024). High capacity clinical SARS-CoV-2 molecular testing using combinatorial pooling. Communications Medicine, 4, Article 121. doi:10.1038/s43856-024-00531-w .
